items.rationale: Pushing the cup into the bag packs the flour, so the cup holds more flour than the recipe means; the extra flour soaks up the liquid and makes the cake dry and dense.
250 g divided by 125 g per cup is 2 cups.

items.answer: Spoon the flour loosely into the measuring cup without packing it, then sweep the excess off the top with a flat edge.
accepted: Spoon flour into the cup and level it off with a knife
Lightly fill the cup with a spoon and scrape the top flat
items.rationale: A right answer has both parts: the flour goes in loosely with a spoon, not packed, and the top is leveled with a flat edge. Informal wording counts.
A liquid measuring cup has room above the line so the liquid does not spill, and reading it at eye level on a flat surface shows the true level.

items.answer: A weight stays the same however loosely or tightly the ingredient is packed, while the amount in a cup changes with how it was filled.
accepted: Because the amount in a cup depends on how packed it is, but the weight does not
Cups vary with how you fill them and weight does not
items.rationale: A full answer gives the reason: packing changes how much fits in a cup, but not the weight. Saying only that scales are more exact names the conclusion without the reason.
Leaveners are used in small, exact amounts; heaping spoons can add a lot more, and too much baking powder makes the batter rise too fast and collapse, and can leave a bitter taste.
